newsitem.title: USA: Clinton lawyer asks for sex-harassment case delay.
newsitem.headline: Clinton lawyer asks for sex-harassment case delay.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's lawyer argued before the Supreme Court on Monday that a sexual harassment lawsuit should be put on hold until he leaves office because it would distract him from his presidential duties.

While Clinton's lawyer sought temporary presidential immunity from civil lawsuits in all but the most exceptional circumstances, attorneys for Paula Jones, a former Arkansas state employee who accused Clinton of harassing her, replied the president should not be placed above the law.
They asked to be allowed to proceed in a federal court in Arkansas with the $700,000 lawsuit in a case that raises important political and constitutional questions.

Lawyers for the two parties in an encounter that allegedly occurred in an Arkansas hotel room in 1991 argued their cases for one hour before the nine justices while Clinton went about his work at the White House and Jones remained at home in California.
A ruling -- solely on the procedural issue of whether the case may proceed immediately, not on its merits -- was expected before the Supreme Court session ends in June.

The justices vigorously questioned lawyers for both sides and for the Justice Department, which supported Clinton, on whether the president should be protected from civil lawsuits for conduct that occurred before taking office.
Justice Sandra Day O'Connor at one point asked whether a president could delay for eight years -- the maximum time a president can serve -- a routine child custody dispute.

"We are saying we will give Miss Jones her day in court (but) let's not do it now," Clinton lawyer Robert Bennett said in arguing that vulnerability to civil suits for private conduct would open U.S. presidents to unacceptable burdens.
Bennett, and Clinton, seek not only to postpone a trial in the politically embarrassing case but to delay any questioning of Clinton or any witnesses until he leaves office.

Clinton's position was backed by a top Justice Department lawyer, Acting Solicitor General Walter Dellinger, who also said an incumbent president should not have to be distracted from the demands of the office by having to appear in court.

Jones claims that Clinton, then governor of Arkansas, had her summoned to a Little Rock hotel room during a government conference at the hotel in 1991 and, once the two were alone, exposed himself to her and asked her to perform oral sex.
Gilbert Davis, an attorney for Jones, said she should be able to press her lawsuit without further delay, arguing that Jones wants to restore her reputation as soon as possible.
Davis cited a number of potential problems if the case were delayed, saying Jones, Clinton or witnesses could die, the memories of witnesses could fade and documents could be lost.
"Justice delayed is justice denied," he told reporters on the courthouse steps later. "That is what the president would seek to have here -- to delay it, just push it off."
Lawyers for Clinton, who has denied making any unwanted advances, declined to join the impromptu news conference, and they later declined comment on the arguments.

At the White House, presidential spokesman Mike McCurry was generally terse as he discussed the matter. Asked if Clinton had any comment on the suit, the spokesman replied: "None that he shared with me."

Joseph Cammarata, another lawyer representing Jones, left open the possibility of negotiating an out-of-court settlement if Clinton apologised, expressed regret for his conduct and admitted Jones did nothing wrong.
"It's never too late to settle," he told reporters.

Cammarata also complained that women's groups were hypocritical for not supporting Jones like they did former law professor Anita Hill, who in 1991 accused Supreme Court Justice-designate Clarence Thomas of sexual harassment.
Leading women's groups replied that Jones had spurned their offers of help, and said politics had overshadowed women's rights in the case.
Bennett, during the arguments, said Clinton "has spent substantial amounts of time on this case already."
But Justice Antonin Scalia asked why the high court should not wait until the president actually claims the case has taken up so much of his time that he could not appear in court or for questioning.

Scalia expressed scepticism about the Clinton argument that a president has a full-time job and should not be disturbed. "I don't find that terribly persuasive," he said, adding that presidents find time to play golf, for example.
